lesson.menu_desc: Giving and taking feedback after the presentation -- too and enough -- 29 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- The Feedback
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mauricio | Lesson 16 -- The Feedback

listenings.text: Good morning, group four. Here is my feedback on yesterday's presentation. First, the good news. Your recommendation was clear, and the numbers were spot on. Mauricio, your part was concise, and your eye contact was much better than on Monday. Now, the room for improvement. The presentation was too long. You had fifteen minutes and you used twenty-two. The slides had too many words, and the pace at the end was too fast. We could not follow it. And you did not leave enough time for questions. For Friday, please cut five slides, and rehearse with a clock. You are good enough to be the best group in the class.

I was fifty-one years old, and I had never received real feedback in English. After my first presentation, a classmate from Germany said, your ideas are strong, but you speak too fast and you use too many filler words. I wanted to defend myself. Then I remembered my own team at the bank. When I give them feedback, I want them to listen, not to argue. So I said, thank you, I will take that on board. The next day, I spoke more slowly, and I stopped saying, you know, every ten seconds. It was not perfect, but it was clear enough. On the last day, the same classmate said, your pace was spot on. That was the best feedback of my year.

reading.rtitle: Feedback in the Program: How It Works
paras: In most executive programs, every presentation ends with feedback. The professor gives it first, and then your classmates give it. It is short, direct, and in front of the group. For many executives, this is the hardest part of the week, because at work nobody gives them feedback anymore.

Good feedback is specific. "It was good" is not enough. "Your slides were too long" is better. "You had twelve slides, and you only had time for eight" is the best. Most feedback is about the same few things: time, slides, pace, and eye contact. The most common problem is simple: the presentation is too long, and there is not enough time for questions.

When you receive feedback, you don't have to agree with all of it, but you should not argue in the room. Say thank you, and take it on board. If something is not clear enough, ask for an example. Many past participants say the same thing: the feedback was hard to hear, but it was the most useful part of the program.

When you give feedback, start with one thing that was spot on. Then give one point of room for improvement, with a fact. Never give more than two points. If you give too many, the person will not remember any of them.
